\chapter{Through the Day}
\label{ch:ta-through-the-day}
\hlchaptermodality{71}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say get up, sleep, run, wash and play in Tamil, and read the letter \ta{ஓ}.}

Complete TA-C71-play and say all five words of the chapter in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[eḻu]{\ta{எழு} (eḻu) — to get up, to rise}

\label{lesson:TA-C71-rise}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kūrai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{எழு}}
\textbf{\ta{எழு}} (\emph{eḻu}) — \textquotedblleft{}to get up, to rise\textquotedblright{}.

The first verb of the morning: to get up, off the \ta{கட்டில்} you named last chapter. It is also what the sun does.

Look at it hard, because you have seen these two letters before with one more on the end. \ta{எழுது} (\emph{eḻudu}) is \textquotedblleft{}to write\textquotedblright{}. \ta{எழு} is \textquotedblleft{}to rise\textquotedblright{}. Whether the longer one grew out of the shorter is a question this book does not answer, because the dictionaries do not agree on it — and it does not matter yet. What matters is that they are two different verbs, they are one letter apart, and swapping them changes what you said.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things a day is made of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eḻu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eḻu}, then \emph{eḻudu} — and say which one is \textquotedblleft{}write\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tarai}, then say \emph{kūrai}, then say \emph{eḻu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{எழு} mean, and which longer verb starts the same way? (\textquotedblleft{}To get up\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{\ta{எழுது}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tūṅgu]{\ta{தூங்கு} (tūṅgu) — to sleep}

\label{lesson:TA-C71-sleep}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{eḻu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{தூங்கு}}
\textbf{\ta{தூங்கு}} (\emph{tūṅgu}) — \textquotedblleft{}to sleep\textquotedblright{}.

The other end of the day — and the verb behind a noun you already own.

\ta{தூக்கம்} (\emph{tūkkam}) is sleep, the thing. \ta{தூங்கு} is sleeping, the doing. Tamil makes that pair again and again, and once you can hear it you get two words for the price of one: the noun \ta{தூக்கம்} sits still, and the verb \ta{தூங்கு} does something.

Its \textbf{\ta{ங்க}} is the same nasal-plus-\ta{க} you say inside \ta{வாங்கு}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two verbs, and the day has both ends.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tūṅgu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tūkkam}, then \emph{tūṅgu} — the thing, then the doing
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vāṅgu}, then \emph{tūṅgu}, and find the sound they share
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kūrai}, then say \emph{eḻu}, then say \emph{tūṅgu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which is the verb and which is the noun — \ta{தூங்கு} or \ta{தூக்கம்}? (\textbf{\ta{தூங்கு}} is the verb.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ō]{\ta{ஓ} — the letter behind a sign you already read}

\label{lesson:TA-S126-letter-oo}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: before the new shape: which letter did \ta{உ} turn out to be the free-standing half of?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ஓ} — the letter behind a sign you already read}
\textbf{\ta{ஓ}} — \emph{ō}.

You have been reading its \textbf{sign}, \ta{◌ோ}, for a long time: it is the hook on \ta{போ} (\emph{pō}), \textquotedblleft{}go\textquotedblright{}, and it is in \ta{கோலம்} too. This is the other half of the same vowel — the \textbf{independent} shape, used when a word \emph{begins} with the sound.

That is the Tamil pattern you already know from \ta{உ}, met once more. Every vowel has two bodies: a free-standing letter for the front of a word, and a sign for inside one.

The next lesson opens with this letter, which is why it arrives here and not later.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two, and say which is the letter and which is the sign
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ta{ஓ}  ·  \ta{◌ோ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{ஓ} three times, saying \emph{ō} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{போ}} — and point at the sign of this same vowel inside it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eḻu}, then say \emph{tūṅgu}, then name the letter \textbf{\ta{ஓ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{ஓ}? Where does the letter go, and where does the sign \ta{◌ோ} go? (\textbf{Letter} at the start of a word; \textbf{sign} on a consonant inside one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ōḍu]{\ta{ஓடு} (ōḍu) — to run}

\label{lesson:TA-C71-run}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tūṅgu} mean, and which letter did you meet after it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஓடு}}
\textbf{\ta{ஓடு}} (\emph{ōḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}to run\textquotedblright{}.

\textquotedblleft{}To run\textquotedblright{} — and the first word in this book that \textbf{begins} with the letter you met one lesson ago.

It is not only for people. Water runs, and so does a \ta{வண்டி} on a \ta{சாலை}: Tamil uses this same verb for all three, where English would want \textquotedblleft{}flow\textquotedblright{} for one of them.

Two letters, one sign, and you can read every part of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and something is moving.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ōḍu}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ஓடு}}, and point at the letter you learned last lesson
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ōḍu}, then name two things other than a person that can do it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tūṅgu}, then name the letter \textbf{\ta{ஓ}}, then say \emph{ōḍu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{ஓடு}} and say what it means. (\textquotedblleft{}To run\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaḻuvu]{\ta{கழுவு} (kaḻuvu) — to wash}

\label{lesson:TA-C71-wash}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ōḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கழுவு}}
\textbf{\ta{கழுவு}} (\emph{kaḻuvu}) — \textquotedblleft{}to wash\textquotedblright{}.

To wash: hands, a \ta{கிண்ணம்}, the \ta{தரை}.

It carries \textbf{\ta{ழ}}, the curled glide that Tamil kept and named itself with — the \ta{ழ} at the end of \ta{தமிழ்}. You have met it inside \ta{எழுது} and at the front of \ta{கீழே}, and here it sits between two \emph{u} sounds, which is the hardest place to hear it and the best place to practise it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the day has some housework in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kaḻuvu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tamiḻ}, then \emph{kaḻuvu} — the same letter, twice
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kaḻuvu}, then name one thing in this book you could wash
  \item \emph{Recall:} name the letter \textbf{\ta{ஓ}}, then say \emph{ōḍu}, then say \emph{kaḻuvu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is in the middle of \ta{கழுவு}, and where else have you met it? (\textbf{\ta{ழ}} — in \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்}} and \textbf{\ta{எழுது}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viḷaiyāḍu]{\ta{விளையாடு} (viḷaiyāḍu) — to play}

\label{lesson:TA-C71-play}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kaḻuvu} mean, and what did \emph{ōḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{விளையாடு}}
\textbf{\ta{விளையாடு}} (\emph{viḷaiyāḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}to play\textquotedblright{}.

The longest word in this chapter, and it is two words welded together.

The back half is \textbf{\ta{ஆடு}}, which on its own means \textquotedblleft{}to move, to sway, to play\textquotedblright{}. And you already know a completely different \ta{ஆடு}: the goat, from the animal chapter. Same letters, same sound, two unrelated words — Tamil lets them share the spelling and lets the sentence sort it out.

That is the last thing this chapter teaches, and it is bigger than the word: a long Tamil word usually has a short one you already own hiding at one end of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five verbs — get up, sleep, run, wash, play — and one new letter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{viḷaiyāḍu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āḍu} on its own, and name the two things it can mean
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five — \emph{eḻu}, \emph{tūṅgu}, \emph{ōḍu}, \emph{kaḻuvu}, \emph{viḷaiyāḍu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ōḍu}, then say \emph{kaḻuvu}, then say \emph{viḷaiyāḍu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What word is hiding at the end of \ta{விளையாடு}, and what else does it mean? (\textbf{\ta{ஆடு}} — and it is also the \textbf{goat}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
